title: Telegram Guide
heading: Telegram — messages out, and a way in
intro: Connect a bot once and the app can message you: an agent tool the assistant reaches for when you ask to be told something, a flow node that writes the message itself from what the run found, and an endpoint for anything else you build.

The same bot works in reverse. Message it and your own agent answers — same tools, same accounts, same memory as the web chat. "How are my positions", "analyse gold", "close EURUSD" all work from your phone with no app installed.
Setup is one field. Talk to @BotFather in Telegram, send /newbot, paste the token it gives you into a Telegram connection, then message your bot once so it knows where to reply.

sections.title: Your bot
sections.sub: Whether the token works, and where a message would go if one were sent now.
sections.footer: Listening for incoming messages: {listening}. No chat means you have not messaged the bot yet and have not set a Chat ID.

sections.title: Chats your bot knows
sections.sub: A bot only learns a chat when someone writes to it — these are the ones the Telegram node offers you to send to.
sections.empty: None yet — message your bot, or add it to a group and say something.

sections.title: Send a message
sections.sub: A real send, to your real chat — the fastest way to prove the token is right.

inputs.name: chat_id
inputs.label: Chat ID (optional)
inputs.placeholder: Leave blank for your connected chat

endpoints.title: Send a message
endpoints.desc: Sends to the Chat ID on your connection, or — if you left that blank — to wherever you last messaged the bot from. Long messages are split on paragraph boundaries rather than truncated, because Telegram rejects anything over 4096 characters outright.

params.name: chat_id
params.desc: Where to send it — a numeric id, negative for a group, or an @username. Several may be given, comma-separated; each is delivered on its own so one bad id cannot swallow the rest.

params.name: connection
params.desc: Which bot to send as, by the name you gave it. Only needed if you have more than one.

endpoints.title: Connection status
endpoints.desc: Whether a bot is connected, which bot it is, which chat it would reply to, and whether the listener that carries incoming messages to your agent is running.

endpoints.title: Your bots
endpoints.desc: The Telegram connections you have added — what the node's "Send as" picker offers. Signed-in request, not an API key.

endpoints.title: Chats the bot has seen
endpoints.desc: Every chat your bot has been written to, newest first, with the name of the person or group. Telegram has no call that lists a bot's chats, so this is built as messages arrive — which is what lets the node offer a menu instead of asking you to hunt for a numeric id. Signed-in request, not an API key.

notes: The flow node takes plain words, not a template. "Send me the setup and why, short" is the whole configuration — the node has the run's findings in front of it and writes the message from them.

The node can also pick WHICH bot sends and WHICH chats receive — both optional, and both worth leaving alone if you have one bot and one chat. A chat you choose there always beats one the model suggests.
Sending to several chats delivers to each separately, so a chat the bot was removed from is reported without stopping the others.
A chart can be sent as a photo. The assistant passes the image it drew as bytes with the text as its caption, because an image the app rendered has no public URL to link to.

Incoming messages are long-polled, not webhooked. A self-hosted box behind a home router has no public URL for Telegram to call, and long-polling works from behind anything — at rest it is about one request a minute.
Send /reset in the chat to start a new conversation. The last few turns are kept so a follow-up like "and enter" still means something.
Anyone who can message your bot is talking to your agent, with your accounts. Keep the token private, and do not add the bot to a group you do not control.
